problem: Each milestone is drawn as a three-year bar (Unix 1969–1972, C 1973–1976, v1.0 1994–1997) even though every one of them is a single-year event. The bar end years appear nowhere in the text, so a student can read the picture as 'Unix work lasted 1969 to 1972' or 'Linux work lasted 1991 to 1994'.
fix: Draw the bars as point markers at 1969, 1973, 1991 and 1994, or state in the caption that the bar width is only for visibility and does not mean a duration.

problem: The paragraph implies Torvalds released the kernel under the GPL from the start. The first public releases (1991) carried a more restrictive licence; the GPL was adopted a few months later, in 1992, before version 0.12.
fix: Write: 'In 1991 he announced the project; the first public version was small and used a more restrictive licence. He soon moved the kernel to the GNU General Public License, or GPL, in 1992.'

problem: 'This is one form of open source' treats the GPL as simply an open-source licence. The GPL comes from the free-software movement and gives users freedoms; 'open source' is a later, separate term with a different emphasis. Blurring them can confuse a student who later meets both terms.
fix: Write: 'The GPL is a free-software licence; licences of this kind are also counted as open source, though the two terms come from different movements.'

problem: 'Linux is a free Unix-like kernel' leaves 'free' undefined at first use. A student may read it as 'no cost' rather than 'freedom to run, study, change and share', which is the sense meant and the sense the GPL section later explains.
fix: Write: 'Linux is a free (openly licensed, with source code anyone may use and change) Unix-like kernel ...' or move the word 'free' to after the GPL explanation.
